entries.title: Batterygate: iOS throttled iPhones with aged batteries
entries.what_happened: iOS 10.2.1 (Feb 2017) introduced dynamic power management that throttled peak CPU performance on iPhones with chemically aged batteries, without disclosing the change in release notes. The throttling was discovered by Primate Labs' John Poole via benchmark anomalies. Apple admitted the behavior in December 2017, apologized for poor communication, and cut battery replacement prices to $29 through 2018. Dozens of lawsuits were consolidated into In re: Apple Inc. Device Performance Litigation (5:18-md-02827, N.D. Cal.). Apple agreed in March 2020 to pay up to $500 million; payouts (~$92.17 per claim) began January 2024. Apple admitted no legal wrongdoing.

entries.title: Batterygate: 30+ US states settle consumer-fraud claims for $113M
entries.what_happened: More than 30 state attorneys general, led by Arizona AG Mark Brnovich, sued Apple over the same iPhone throttling. Investigators found Apple acted deceptively by hiding the shutdown/slowdown issues and that the slowdown 'potentially' boosted iPhone sales 'by millions of devices per year'. Apple agreed to pay $113 million. As part of the deal Apple did not admit to breaking any laws.

entries.title: Italy AGCM fines Apple EUR10M and Samsung EUR5M for planned obsolescence
entries.what_happened: Italy's competition authority (AGCM) found both companies pushed firmware updates that caused 'serious malfunctions' and 'significantly reduced performance' on older devices, accelerating replacement. Samsung pushed Galaxy Note 4 owners to install an Android build designed for the Note 7 without warning of hardware stress. Apple pushed iPhone 6 users toward iOS 10 (optimized for iPhone 7) and later iOS 10.2.1 throttling, without informing users of energy demands or shutdown risks, and offered no way to restore prior functionality. Apple received two EUR5M fines (one for the updates, one for failing to inform customers about battery maintenance/replacement); Samsung received EUR5M.

entries.title: France DGCCRF fines Apple EUR25M for undisclosed iPhone throttling
entries.what_happened: Following a complaint by the Halt Planned Obsolescence (HOP) association, France's DGCCRF investigated and found iPhone owners were not informed that iOS 10.2.1 and 11.2 updates could slow their devices. Because users cannot downgrade iOS, many were forced to replace batteries or buy new phones. DGCCRF ruled the omission a 'misleading commercial practice by omission'. Apple agreed to pay EUR25 million and to publish a press release about the fine on its website for one month.

entries.title: Epson printers brick on waste-ink counter 'end of service life'
entries.what_happened: Epson inkjet printers track waste ink with an internal counter. When the counter hits a preset limit, the printer displays 'a printer's ink pad is at the end of its service life' and refuses to print at all — even if the physical pad is not saturated. A July 2022 viral tweet by University of New Haven lecturer Mark Tavern sparked press coverage. Epson confirmed the mechanism (ink-pad saturation risk) and updated its support page to point users at its Maintenance Reset Utility; it also noted paid ink-pad replacement service. Critics note the trigger is a software counter, resettable with third-party tools, and the lockout arrives with no advance warning.

entries.title: Sonos 'Recycle Mode' permanently bricked traded-in speakers
entries.what_happened: Sonos's Trade Up program offered 30% off new gear but required the old device be placed in 'Recycle Mode' via the app, starting an irreversible 21-day countdown after which the speaker was permanently deactivated (server-side blacklisted) — even though the hardware was fully functional. E-waste recycler Devin Wilson publicized cases of working Play:5 units rendered un-resellable. Sonos defended the practice on user-experience grounds, then quietly removed Recycle Mode from the app (reported March 2020); Trade Up now requires only the serial number, and a factory reset leaves hardware functional.

entries.title: HP firmware updates blocked third-party ink via 'Dynamic Security'
entries.what_happened: HP's Dynamic Security cartridge-authentication system, delivered through firmware updates (including a November 2020 push), made printers reject fully functional third-party ink/toner lacking HP's security chip — often without warning, after users had already bought the hardware and supplies. A December 2020 US class action (Mobile Emergency Housing Corp. et al.) alleged the updates functioned as unauthorized code changes under computer-crime law. Settlement reached August 2024 and approved by Judge Susan Van Keulen in March 2025: no admission of wrongdoing, no class-wide payouts (three representatives received $5,000 each; ~$725,000 in fees), but owners of 21 listed models can now decline Dynamic Security updates or downgrade. An FTC proposed consent order (reported March 2026) would go further, barring similar restrictions without clear pre-purchase disclosure.

evidence_labels.confirmed: Court filing, regulator decision, or company admission establishes the facts.
evidence_labels.likely: Reputable reporting with company acknowledgment of the mechanism; no court or regulator ruling on record.

methodology: Each entry documents a case where a manufacturer used software or firmware to degrade, disable, or brick older hardware. Evidence labels: 'confirmed' = the mechanism or penalty is established by a court filing, regulator decision, or the company's own admission; 'likely' = reported by reputable press with company acknowledgment of the underlying mechanism but no court or regulator ruling. Only cases with real, verifiable sources are included.
